transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Time: 15:00 - 15:38 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Solaris Head of ML), Carlos Mendez (Solaris Backend), Leah Thompson (Solaris CTO)

Auto-generated summary: quick hosted API demo focusing on chat and text generation. Some transcription artifacts expected.

00:00 Alex Morales: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat and text generation basics, streaming and retry behavior. Samir's gonna drive the demo, i'll chime in on pricing and next steps - okay?
00:12 Priya Raman: sounds good, thanks Alex, quick context - we're prototyping a customer support assistant and some transactional messaging, latency's big for some endpoints, cost matters but reliability and audit logs are must-haves for compliance.
00:25 Alex Morales: great, that's helpful. Samir, want to start on the console and the simple API call?
00:31 Samir Patel: yeah, sure. i'm sharing my screen - can folks see the Redwood console?
00:36 Carlos Mendez: yep seeing it. little lag but fine.
00:40 Samir Patel: ok great. so first, the hosted API has a simple REST interface for text and chat. here's a chat example curl: post to /v1/chat with messages array, model param, temperature, top_p, max_tokens. streaming is supported via server-sent events, so you can stream tokens as they arrive.
01:05 Priya Raman: do you support partial replies, like token-by-token or chunked?
01:09 Samir Patel: yes. streaming comes as SSE events with data: chunks. you can buffer or render incrementally. we also have SDKs that wrap streaming for common languages - node, python, go. note streaming reduces end-to-end latency for the first token because you don't wait for full decode.
01:29 Leah Thompson: how do retries work with streaming? like if a connection drops mid-stream do you have idempotency keys?
01:36 Samir Patel: good question. we recommend using idempotency tokens on the request. for short transient network issues, the SDK will retry at the transport level; for resumed streaming we give guidance - typically client should re-issue request with same idempotency key and the server can use prefix caching to resume if the prefix was committed to cache. it's not perfect resume for every model, but for many chat flows prefix caching reduces duplicate tokens.
02:01 Alex Morales: to add, our platform supports automatic prefix/KV cache which helps with retries and reduces cost for repeated prompts. we can also route to a compatible model variant if the original model isn't available during retry.
02:13 Priya Raman: nice. can you show an example of temperature and top_p differences? we need determinism for some transactional messages.
02:20 Samir Patel: sure - so temperature 0 to 0.2 is great for deterministic output; top_p also narrows sampling. i'll show a side-by-side of two calls - temp 0 vs temp 0.8.
02:30 [demo: two requests sent, streaming visible]
02:36 Priya Raman: ok temp 0 looks tight, temp .8 is more creative. good, we need deterministic templates for receipts and variable responses for suggestions.
02:45 Carlos Mendez: what about token limits and truncation, do you have recommendations for prompt engineering to stay within budgets?
02:52 Samir Patel: yes, we expose model context length in the catalog; we also surface token usage per request in the console. best practices: trim system messages, chunk long documents and use embeddings for retrieval rather than sending full docs in prompt. batching and caching reduce unit cost.
03:10 Leah Thompson: security - data retention and SOC2 - do hosted customers get logs or are we able to opt-out of retention?
03:17 Alex Morales: we are SOC 2 compliant; hosted defaults to short retention but we offer enterprise options for retention controls. for sensitive workloads you can use Private deployment or Dedicated capacity with customer-managed KMS. we can provide the SOC2 report and our security whitepaper.
03:33 Priya Raman: do you encrypt at rest with customer KMS?
03:36 Alex Morales: yes, enterprise plans support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and audit logs with RBAC. we'll share the security deck after the call.
03:45 Priya Raman: thanks. also curious about rate limits - we expect bursts around payroll runs, and synchronous low-latency for chat. what's the burst behavior?
03:53 Samir Patel: hosted has tiered quotas; default free tiers are modest, paid tiers get much higher concurrency. for bursty production we recommend Dedicated or reserved throughput and burst capacity, but hosted does support higher quotas on request. autoscaling varies by deployment, hosted allows soft burst through policy.
04:15 Carlos Mendez: for latency-sensitive calls, are there specific SLAs?
04:19 Alex Morales: hosted has latency targets per model class, we publish performance profiles in the model catalog. Dedicated can give more predictable SLOs. for highly latency-sensitive paths you can also pin lightweight quantized variants tuned for low p99 latency.
04:35 Priya Raman: you mentioned quantization - does hosted support quantized models or is that only for Dedicated/Private?
04:40 Samir Patel: hosted supports certain optimized model variants we vet; we do run quantized variants in our hosted fleet where they make sense. Dedicated gives you more control over specific kernel options and quant settings.
04:55 [demo moves to SDK sample code]
05:02 Samir Patel: here's a node example for streaming with the SDK - you register an event handler for token events, handle end and error events, and pass an idempotency key for safe retries. code sample also shows automatic exponential backoff for transient 5xx.
05:24 Priya Raman: if an SDK retry duplicates tokens, how do we dedupe downstream?
05:29 Samir Patel: best practice is to include the idempotency key and message sequence id in your business payload, so you can dedupe at the application layer. we also surface request ids in logs for tracing.
05:44 Carlos Mendez: can we get per-token cost estimates in the console? that would help run our cost budgets.
05:50 Alex Morales: yes, console shows token breakdown per request and cost estimates; Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and caching to reduce costs for common workload patterns.
06:02 Priya Raman: what's the onboarding flow if we want to trial? is there a free tier or a time-limited trial?
06:08 Alex Morales: we offer trial credits and a 2-week trial for hosted with a temporary key. during trial we can also run a small benchmark to estimate costs. for production we'd propose a usage-based plan or a reserved commit for Dedicated.
06:20 Leah Thompson: demo looks solid. any pitfalls integrating with our auth? we use SSO (SAML) and have strict IP allowlists.
06:28 Alex Morales: for hosted we support SSO for console access and SAML for orgs; for API access you'll manage keys but we integrate with orgs and can do IP allowlists for API keys for extra control, otherwise Dedicated/Private allow more network controls.
06:42 Priya Raman: can you do region pinning for data residency? we have EU customers.
06:46 Samir Patel: yes, hosted supports region selection, and Private gives full region control. we can arrange EU-only routing for EU workloads.
06:55 [short pause as demo loads]
07:02 Samir Patel: back to retry patterns - let me show the JSON structure we return for errors: you get structured error codes for rate_limit, unavailable, model_error. for rate_limit the header includes retry-after. SDKs interpret retry-after and do backoff.
07:20 Carlos Mendez: if we get a 429 mid-stream is that considered partial success? do you have idempotent streaming semantics?
07:26 Samir Patel: 429 mid-stream is typically partial, so client should either resume with idempotency key and check prefix cache or re-request full generation depending on your tolerance for duplicates. we also support streaming with checkpoints in certain SDKs to aid resume.
07:45 Priya Raman: let's talk about a real integration scenario - chat for support plus auto-generated receipts. the receipts must be deterministic and auditable. suggestions can be fuzzy. how would you set up two different model routes?
07:58 Alex Morales: you can set up per-route model pinning and route policy - low-latency deterministic route pinned to a 0-temp variant, and a separate exploratory route with higher temp. Console supports per-route quotas, tracing, and canaries for rollouts.
08:18 Leah Thompson: do you keep prompts in logs? for audits we need request and response hashes without storing raw PII.
08:26 Alex Morales: default logs are redacted for PII; for enterprises we can provide hashed request/response storage or no-retention options. we can discuss data governance in more detail with security team.
08:40 Priya Raman: also curious about how you measure output quality and regressions - we need to ensure updates don't degrade accuracy for our templates.
08:47 Samir Patel: Redwood Optimize includes evaluation harnesses and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets; you can create test prompts and get regression alerts when a model update changes outputs beyond thresholds.
08:58 Carlos Mendez: sounds useful. moving to latency numbers - do you have example p50/p95 for the model class we demoed?
09:05 Samir Patel: for the small-ish conversational model we demoed p50 is ~80-120ms token start on our hosted fleet in us-west, p95 varies by context length but typical p95 first-token around 400-600ms. we'll include specific numbers per model in the catalog.
09:25 Priya Raman: that aligns with what we need for suggestions, but for real-time chat we may need sub-200ms p95. is that achievable?
09:32 Alex Morales: for sub-200ms p95 you typically need Dedicated with pinned capacity, optimized model variant, and smaller context windows. we can run a benchmark and show what config meets your p95 goal.
09:47 Leah Thompson: what's the expected engineering lift to integrate, how long for PoC?
09:51 Alex Morales: for a basic PoC using hosted API, a couple engineers could have a prototype in a week; for benchmarked production with SLAs maybe 4-8 weeks including security review.
10:04 [demo continues: console usage, logs]
10:25 Samir Patel: quick note on quotas again - we also provide per-route throttles so you can shape traffic to protect critical paths.
10:33 Priya Raman: are there sample configs for quotas and autoscaling we can reuse?
10:37 Samir Patel: yes, we'll share recommended policy templates for chat workloads and for high-throughput batch inference.
10:45 Carlos Mendez: do you integrate with observability stacks? we use Datadog and Sentry.
10:50 Alex Morales: we provide tracing hooks and exportable metrics - Datadog, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry integrations available for enterprise customers.
10:58 Priya Raman: anything else on retries? we have idempotency per message but many of our flows are multi-turn. how do you recommend storing conversation state?
11:08 Samir Patel: store conversation state client-side or in your DB and pass only the short context necessary. Redwood supports KV/prefix cache to avoid resending large history; you can reference cached vectors or conversation fragments. for long-term state, keep canonical state in your DB and hydrate short context for the model.
11:28 Priya Raman: ok makes sense. are there any limits on streaming concurrently per key?
11:34 Samir Patel: concurrency quotas exist per org and per key; we can raise them for trial and production as needed. for extremely high concurrency we'd often recommend Dedicated.
11:44 [customer asks about reliability during deployments]
11:48 Alex Morales: we support canary rollouts, automatic fallback policies to a compatible model variant, and per-route circuit breakers that can route traffic to a lower-cost or lower-latency fallback.
11:59 Priya Raman: great. can you share the SRE runbook for incidents?
12:03 Alex Morales: yes we'll share a sanitized SRE runbook and incident process doc.
12:08 [short technical deep-dive from Samir about streaming internals]
12:10 Samir Patel: under the hood streaming uses chunked responses and we maintain a KV cache of token prefixes to support cheap retries; kernel selection and batching are per-request, and for models that support it we use attention optimizations to reduce compute. sometimes transcript may say kubenets or kubernetis - currently we orchestrate on k8s with custom autoscaler, but that's an internal detail.
12:36 Priya Raman: perfect. one more on cost: can we run a small benchmark and get a cost projection? we have typical traffic estimates per day.
12:44 Alex Morales: yes, we can run a benchmark during your trial period and produce cost modeling - Samir we'll coordinate the benchmark plan.
12:51 Samir Patel: noted, i'll prepare a benchmark checklist: dataset, request patterns, concurrency, target latency, and quality metrics.
13:02 [fast-forward through demo steps, occasional cross-talk and short interruptions]
22:10 Priya Raman: quick interruption - sorry i had to step away, i'm back.
22:20 Carlos Mendez: no worries.
22:27 Samir Patel: we're now showing the trace view in the console - you can see per-request latency, token counts, and error codes. we also have a queryable audit log for enterprise customers.
22:45 Priya Raman: that UI looks helpful. can the logs be exported to our S3 for long-term retention?
22:51 Alex Morales: yes, we support log exporting to customer S3 buckets and also direct hooks to SIEMs.
22:58 Leah Thompson: ok let's recap and next steps.
23:03 Alex Morales: recap - we'll send pricing, hosted vs dedicated comparison, SOC2 and security whitepaper, and a trial key for a 2-week benchmark. Samir will share streaming/retry code samples and a benchmark checklist. Priya will share internal success criteria and a list of engineers for access. schedule benchmarking for week of 2026-05-04.
23:28 Priya Raman: all good. one final question - do you support function/tool calling or structured outputs? some of our flows need JSON output enforcement.
23:38 Samir Patel: yes, we support function calling and structured output enforcement; plus schema validation helpers in SDKs. for strict JSON outputs we recommend temperature 0, top_p low, and post-parse validation.
23:58 Carlos Mendez: thanks, that answers my technical questions.
24:05 Leah Thompson: thanks for the thorough demo.
24:08 Alex Morales: thank you all. we'll follow up with the materials.
24:12 Priya Raman: thanks, talk soon.
